analysis.one_liner: Replaces state product liability laws with a federal standard that makes it harder to sue manufacturers for defective products.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in House committees when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overridden state product liability laws with one national standard. Injured people could only win if they proved a manufacturer was careless — not just that the product was unreasonably dangerous, which is the strict liability rule most states use. It would also have made it harder to win punitive damages and reduced any award by the workers' compensation benefits the injured person received. The bill was referred to two House committees, then to subcommittees, and was never taken up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and product sellers, who would face fewer and weaker lawsuits from people injured by defective products. Liability insurers would also benefit from smaller, less predictable payouts. The bill's uniform standard would mean companies no longer face stricter rules in states like California or New Jersey.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces state strict liability with a negligence-only test for defective design and failure-to-warn claims, so an injured person must prove the manufacturer failed to act as a reasonable manufacturer would, rather than simply that the product was unreasonably dangerous [S2][S3].
Preempts inconsistent state laws nationwide, ending stricter liability rules in individual states and giving manufacturers one uniform standard [S2][S3].

Requires clear and convincing evidence of reckless disregard before punitive damages can be awarded, and lists factors — including the company's financial condition — that limit how large such awards can be [S2][S3].
Reduces any damages award by the amount of workers' compensation benefits paid or payable for the same injury, lowering manufacturers' total exposure [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products, who would bear a heavier burden of proof, smaller recoveries offset by workers' compensation, and no recourse to whatever stricter protections their state had provided. State laws giving consumers stronger remedies would be wiped out.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override stronger state consumer protections, so people in states with strict liability laws could no longer recover for an unreasonably dangerous product unless they could prove negligence [S2][S3].

Deducting workers' compensation benefits from any court award means an injured worker's total recovery is capped at roughly the cost of the injury, not the full harm, and employers lose their ability to be repaid through subrogation [S2][S3].

The bill's backers would have argued it fixes real problems: a patchwork of 50 state liability standards raises costs that get passed to consumers, and punitive damages can be unpredictable and impose liability without fault. The bill did include some protections for claimants, such as holding sellers liable when the actual manufacturer cannot be sued, and letting injured workers keep awards free of employer liens [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one-national-standard argument had some force, but its core effect was to shift risk away from manufacturers and onto injured consumers: a harder legal test, harder-to-win punitive damages, and reduced recoveries. Notably, it carved environmental and toxic-contamination cases out entirely, which narrowed the injury claims it affected to ordinary consumer and workplace injuries [S2][S3]. The bill was extremely narrow in support — no cosponsors at all — and died without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 1991, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, sent to their subcommittees within two weeks, and never taken up again before Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Toby Roth (R-WI) introduced the Product Liability Uniform Standards Act on July 17, 1991; it had zero cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred the same day to both the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee [S5].

Within two weeks it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness — the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
Neither committee ever held a markup or brought the bill to a vote, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers kept their existing state-law rights to sue manufacturers, including strict liability rules the bill would have eliminated. Manufacturers and their insurers gained nothing from the bill's failure, since the status quo they wanted changed remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers and state tort law

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 17, 1991, passed it to a subcommittee on July 26, and never scheduled a markup or floor action.

against.what_they_did: Received a joint referral on July 17, 1991, passed it to a subcommittee on July 23, and never scheduled a markup or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party; the Democratic-controlled committees that held the bill never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced state strict liability with a negligence test, made punitive damages much harder to win, and cut damages by workers' comp offsets — all reducing what manufacturers pay people injured by their products [S2][S3].
A uniform negligence standard with restricted punitive damages would mean smaller and more predictable payouts on injury claims [S2][S3].
Harder proof standards, federal preemption, and a study panel reviewing attorney fees would shrink the pool of viable injury cases lawyers could take on contingency [S2][S3].
The bill would have barred employers and workers' comp insurers from subrogation liens against injured workers' recoveries, so they could not be repaid from a lawsuit award [S3].
